entries.title: Room for their own movement
entries.invitation: The authors make room for the baby’s own awake movement, with comfort and help close by.
entries.summary: The authors favor awake movement that the baby initiates, with room to explore, help when needed, and no propping into sitting or standing before they can get there themselves.
entries.cue: Notice how your baby moves now, what catches their attention, and when effort becomes frustration.
detail: Davies and Uzodike describe a prepared space where a baby can explore their own movements. A nearby object may invite a reach or a change of direction; the point is to follow the baby’s present interest and pace.

Their caution is about propping a baby into sitting or standing. They separately describe awake time on both the back and tummy, while noticing discomfort and changing things or picking the baby up when needed.

When effort turns to frustration, they describe coming closer and offering enough help for the baby to continue. Their activity ages are guides, and they explicitly welcome seeking support for developmental concerns.

detail: Come where your baby can see your face. Say something, listen, and leave a little space for their sound or movement. You can echo a sound, smile back, or put a few words to what seems to interest them.
Raspberries, bubbles and changes in volume are part of the vocal play the authors describe. There is no need to ask for a particular sound or word.

entries.title: Learning to use a fork, spoon and glass
entries.summary: The books describe letting a child take over parts of eating as coordination grows, with small, manageable tools and adult help. Food and cutlery stay at the table.

entries.title: When your baby hits, bites, pushes or throws
entries.summary: When a baby hits, bites, pushes or throws, the authors look for what the movement might communicate while keeping a kind, clear limit on hurting. The adult helps when feelings are too strong for words.
entries.cue: Your baby is showing a strong preference through their movements, and someone or something may be hurt.
detail: The book describes some babies showing stronger preferences around nine to twelve months. A hit might follow unwanted handling; a push might mean wanting to get past. A bite might come with hunger, upset or teething. These are questions to consider, not certain explanations.

Throwing can be a different kind of exploration: the object may be too easy or difficult, or the baby may be interested in how it falls. The authors look for another way to explore that is not dangerous or disruptive. Their boundaries chapter gives a basket of suitable balls as one alternative to throwing an unsuitable object.

The adult stops hurtful actions and can move with the baby away from the situation when needed. During intense crying, the authors use few words, offer a cuddle if wanted and stay nearby if touch is refused.

After calm returns, they give a short explanation and model repair, such as offering a tissue to someone who was hurt or putting thrown things back. They describe babies watching this before taking more of a part as toddlers.
For repeated situations, the book looks at what happened just before, including noise, crowding, a difficult transition or an activity’s fit. Adjusting those conditions is another way to help.

entries.title: Welcoming a baby or adopted child
entries.summary: The Baby authors describe time to get to know each other after birth or adoption. They include support for the adults, room for feelings of love that take time, and a doctor’s help when needed for postpartum depression.
entries.cue: When a newborn arrives, or an adopted child joins your family.
detail: The authors call the first six to eight weeks after birth “symbiosis,” or life together. Ordinary care, talking, singing, and noticing a baby’s rhythms are ways of becoming familiar with one another.

They suggest simplifying social commitments where possible and accepting practical help. They also recognize that a quiet home may be difficult with older siblings, and that help depends on the people and resources available to each family.

For adoption, they suggest a similar period of getting acquainted whenever the child arrives. Familiar voices, gentle care, and predictable places and rhythms are their focus. Their six-to-eight-week suggestion describes time together; it is not an attachment deadline.

The authors explicitly include caregivers who did not carry the baby, parents who return to work soon after birth, and families who do not breastfeed. They acknowledge that love may not feel immediate and direct parents toward a doctor when needed for postpartum depression, alongside accepting support from others.

entries.summary: Both books value attention during ordinary time together. Davies acknowledges competing commitments and offers ways to turn toward a child without expecting an adult to attend to everything at once.

detail: The Baby authors suggest using care as time to connect, and sometimes simply holding and enjoying a baby without another purpose. These can be moments within the day you already have.

entries.title: Notice your own limit before it builds
entries.summary: Davies suggests noticing an approaching limit and expressing it kindly before irritation builds. The Baby authors also invite reflection on the adult’s own needs, without turning it into a judgment of their parenting.

detail: Notice what you are feeling and what you need, as well as what your child needs. Davies describes adult limits as part of balancing the people in a family, and says that following the child leaves room for the adult too.

entries.title: Take turns hearing each other out
entries.summary: For an everyday disagreement with a trusted caregiver who is willing to talk, Davies offers a listening exercise: hear their concern, reflect back what you understood, invite correction, then switch roles.

detail: Davies adapts an exercise from Scilla Elworthy’s 2017 Montessori Congress address. She proposes asking whether the other person has twenty minutes: five for them to speak, five for you to reflect what you heard, then the same two turns with the roles reversed.
